scenes.tts: Cells carry cargo, pull chromosomes apart and shorten muscles, and the workers are motor proteins. A motor is an enzyme that turns A T P into steps along a track. The tracks are actin filaments and microtubules, and each track has a direction. Myosins walk on actin. Kinesins and dyneins walk on microtubules. So which motor goes which way, and how do we know?
scenes.visual: A cell outline with a microtubule and an actin bundle; three motor icons appear, each labelled with its family.
scenes.narration: Cells carry cargo, pull chromosomes apart and shorten muscles, and the workers are motor proteins. A motor is an enzyme that turns ATP into steps along a track. The tracks are actin filaments and microtubules, and each track has a direction. Myosins walk on actin. Kinesins and dyneins walk on microtubules. So which motor goes which way, and how do we know?

scenes.tts: Most myosins move toward the barbed end of actin. Kinesin one moves toward the plus end of a microtubule, so it carries cargo outward. Cytoplasmic dynein moves toward the minus end, so it carries cargo inward. But the family does not always give the direction. Myosin six, and a fly protein called n c d, are exceptions. Direction has to be measured for each motor.
scenes.visual: Two polar tracks with arrows for plus and minus ends; kinesin and dynein icons move opposite ways; myosin VI and ncd flagged as exceptions.
scenes.narration: Most myosins move toward the barbed end of actin. Kinesin-1 moves toward the plus end of a microtubule, so it carries cargo outward. Direction has to be measured for each motor.

scenes.tts: How does one motor move? Kinesin one has two heads that alternate, hand over hand. One head holds on while the other moves, so the motor is processive. It takes many steps without letting go. The cargo advances eight nanometres per step, and each step costs one A T P at low load. These numbers come from purified proteins, in vitro.
scenes.visual: Two-headed kinesin stepping along a microtubule; a green ATP chip spent at each 8 nm step; an in vitro label.

scenes.tts: To watch one motor step, use an optical trap. A focused laser holds a small bead, and a bead pulled off centre feels a force, like a weight on a spring. The force is the stiffness times the distance. In a trap, kinesin beads advanced in eight nanometre steps, and the motor kept going against loads up to five to six piconewtons. With made up numbers, a stiffness of zero point zero five piconewtons per nanometre and a stall at one hundred twenty nanometres give six piconewtons.
scenes.visual: Bead in a laser trap, spring and force arrow growing as the bead stalls; F = 0.05 x 120 = 6 pN.

scenes.tts: Motors rarely work alone. In reconstitution experiments, purified human dynein becomes a fast, processive motor when it binds dynactin and an activating adaptor, a protein that also binds cargo. Some adaptors recruit two dyneins, and that gave more force. In muscle, millions of myosin heads each pull once and let go. The thin filaments slide past the thick ones, so no filament gets shorter.
scenes.visual: Dynein with dynactin and an adaptor bound to a vesicle; then a sarcomere shortening with constant thick filament length.

scenes.tts: Keep three things. Motors turn A T P into steps along polar tracks. The family gives the track, but the direction is measured for each motor. And every number belongs to the preparation that measured it: one motor, in vitro, under the loading condition that was measured.
